Synthesis of (+)-Hypoxylactone through Allenoate γ‑Addition:
Revision of Stereochemistry
Gyungah Pak, Euijin Park, Saehansaem Park, and Jimin Kim *
Cite This: J. Org. Chem. 2020, 85, 14246 −14252 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A synthesis of (+)-hypoxylactone has been
accomplished in four steps starting from the allenoate γ-addition
of threo-3-chloro-2-silyoxybutanals, leading to the revision of
stereochemistry. The key was the discovery of control elements
required to matching/mismatching cases in the allenoate γ-
addition to provide the desired adducts as a single isomer. The
utility of the γ-adduct was demonstrated with the Au(I)-catalyzed
cyclization to a ﬀord (+)-xylogiblactone A. Use of Ag
2O was the
key to epoxidation for preventing epimerization of the γ-lactone
ring.
T
arget-oriented synthesis (TOS) becomes an important
concept to provide natural products and their derivatives
in an eﬃcient way.1 Due to scarcity in nature, TOS is crucial to
increase access to natural products often identi ﬁed as bioactive
substances. This protocol can supply both natural and unnatural
compounds in quantity and allow continuing biological studies
to unveil new properties and functions. 2 Ideally, concise
syntheses with perfect regio- and stereoselectivity providing a
single product o ﬀer e ﬃcient and practical tools to achieve the
ultimate goal.
Structurally unique γ-lactone polyketide (+)-hypoxylactone
(1) was isolated from the fermentation broth of marine fungus
Hypoxylon croceum found in a mangrove estuary drift wood
along with several sordarins including hypoxysordarin (2).
3 The
new sordarin derivatives enable selective inhibition of protein
synthesis, resulting in antifungal activity. In the plausible
biological pathway, the initial step with the side chain in
hypoxysordarin gives an acetal enzyme complex through a
nucleophilic addition of a hydrolase onto the ester. The release
of hypoxylactone together with sordarin can be catalyzed by the
hydrolase through an epoxide opening event as illustrated in
Figure 1 . The structure of hypoxylactone ( 1) was deduced by
comparison with NMR data of co-occurring hypoxysordarin
(2). To the best of our knowledge, only similar polyketides from
natural butenolides
4 are antifungal xylogiblactones A, B, and C
isolated from a di ﬀerent fermented broth of Xylotunulus
gibbisporus YMJ863 in 2014. 5 In this respect, it is possible that
the side chain bearing a cis-epoxide in hypoxylactone ( 1) could
be derived from a chlorohydrin unit in xylogiblactone A ( 4)o r
vice versa ( Figure 1).
In view of stereochemical connection for both natural γ-
lactone polyketides, we were intrigued by the fact that
hypoxylactone ( 1) correlates with non-natural xylogiblactone
A( 4), but its epimer, unnatural 6,7- epi-xylogiblactone A ( 3)i n
the biological or chemical phenomenon. This could be de ﬁned
as an unusual case in spite of the di ﬀerent origins of natural
sources for 1 and 4.
Allene has been proved to be a useful functionality for a variety
of transition-metal catalysis, particularly for cyclizations in the
construction of carbo- and heterocycles.
6 Recently, we disclosed

a novel procedure of asymmetric allenoate γ-addition reactions
to provide γ-adducts in the construction of axial and center
chirality simultaneously.7 The γ-adduct is readily amenable for
further conversion to heterocyclic synthetic intermediates
including γ-lactones by gold catalysis.
8 Concise synthesis of
(+)-xylogiblactone A ( 4) through the allenoate γ-addition of
unprecedented kinetic resolution of racemic aldehydes clearly
demonstrates the eﬃcacy and applicability of this methodology.
9
The characteristic features of this approach, in terms of the
chemical eﬃciency of the unusual stereoselective assembly and
the structural features of the products, have prompted us to carry
out further investigations as depicted in Scheme 1 . It was
envisaged that syntheses of 3 and 4, potential precursors for
hypoxylactone, could be realized in a predictable fashion by the
allenoate γ-additions with chiral aldehydes 7 and 8.
Herein, we wish to describe concise syntheses of 3 and 4,
demonstrating the utility of the allenoateγ-addition reaction and
the correlation between two natural products, hypoxylactone
(1) and xylogiblactone A ( 4). This investigation led to the
correction and veri ﬁcation of the known relative and absolute
stereochemistry of hypoxylactone ( 1).
With this issue in mind, we began with readily available
L- and
D-threonines for the preparation of starting chiral aldehydes 7
and 8 in quantity, as modiﬁed and improved literature procedure
(Scheme 2 ).10 First, the cis-epoxide 10 was obtained in three
steps from D-threonine: the transformations ﬁrst involved
diazotization and bromination of D-threonine. The resulting
bromohydrine was converted to an epoxidation under basic
conditions, and then the carboxylate was treated with Me
2SO4 to
produce the desired epoxy ester 10. Early trials for the epoxide
opening reaction of 10 with TiCl 4 or SnCl 4 under various
conditions11 indicated that the conversion to the desired
chlorohydrin 11 could not be satis ﬁed presumably due to a
lack of reactivity. Although the reaction produced 11,i ts uﬀered
from low yield (13%) and several impurities.12 We subsequently
considered that a Lewis base catalyst, such as HMPA, DMF, or
DMP, previously utilized for a variety of transformations
through increasing reactivity of Lewis acid,
13 could be employed
for this transformation. Fortunately, utilization of NMP ( N-
methylpyrrolidone, 1.0 equiv) with TiCl4 (1.2 equiv) at −78 °C
cleanly provided 11 in 89% yield as a single isomer, not only
increasing the reactivity but also improving chemical yields viaA
in Scheme 2 . The resulting ester 11 was converted to the
aldehyde 7a through a reduction using Dibal-H (2.1 equiv) at
−78 °C for 30 min after the protection of a hydroxyl group by
TBS.
The stage was thus set for theγ-addition reaction of 6 with the
aldehydes 7 or 8 mediated by chiral bromoborane 5.14 Initial
attempts of the allenoate γ-addition of 6 to 7a (P = TBS) could
not be realized under various conditions. The reaction of 6 with
(R,R)-5, prepared in situ from (1R,2R)-1,2-diphenylethane-1,2-
bis-tosylsulfonamide and BBr3, in the presence of i-Pr2NEt (2.1
equiv) at −50 °C for 30 min in CH2Cl2, followed by the addition
of 7a at −20 °C indicated that the conversion to the γ-adduct
completely failed, owing to a lack of reactivity caused by a
geometrical issue. This is not a surprising outcome based on the
analysis of the reaction pathway depicted in Scheme 3.
In fact, the low reactivity can be predictable by stereo-
electronic e ﬀects and geometrical preference: Stereochemical
model B, considered as the Felkin −Anh model, could be
electronically favored due to an interaction of the π*
C=O orbital
with an adjacent perpendicular σ*C−O orbital, lowering the
LUMO energy level. 15 However, a severe steric interaction in
model B exists between R and Me, leading to a mismatching pair
in the stereochemical interaction.16 We subsequently speculated
that the modi ﬁcation of 7a might be required to reduce steric
bulkiness. Accordingly, the TBS group was replaced with a
smaller TMS group. After surveying several conditions with 7b,
several key ﬁndings emerged: (1) an enolization time for 30 min
at −50 °C was crucial for optimal conditions ( Table 1, entry 4
and entries 1∼4); (2) reactions performed at −10 °Ci nC H
2Cl2
resulted in the best chemical yields in comparison with other
solvents, including toluene and a mixed solvent system (Table 1,
entries 7 and 8). Although 12 was produced during the reaction,
the low chemical yield (11%) remained to be improved ( Table
1, entry 3). Fortunately, we were delighted to ﬁnd an optimal
condition, which is the reaction of 6 with 5a in the presence of i-
Pr2NEt at −50 °C for 30 min, and then the addition of7b at −50
°C warming up to −10 °C for 4 h to give the γ-adduct 12 in 34%
isolated yield as a single regio- and stereoisomer ( Table 1, entry
4).
Although the exact mechanistic aspects of this transformation
have not been rigorously elucidated, Scheme 3 illustrates
possible stereochemical routes B and C for the γ-allenoate
addition adduct. Due to a severe steric repulsion between R and
Me in electronically favored the Felkin −Anh model B, model B

could be converted to the more sterically stable model C.W e
believe that the origin of the stereochemical outcomes for 12 via
γ-addition might be a subtle geometrical preference for the
orientation sterically less demanding in model C.
It is worth noting that γ-adduct 12 is a key intermediate to
construct the reported structure of hypoxylactone ( 1). Next, a
regiospeciﬁc oxacyclization of 12 was conducted under the
conditions of gold catalysts to form the γ-lactone moiety (Table
2). After investigations for optimizing the cyclization, the use of
Ph3PAuNTf2 proved to be superior to other gold catalysts
(Table 2, entries 4 and 5). The cyclization of 12 in the presence
of Ph3PAuNTf2 (10 mol %) at 0 °C for 1 h in CH2Cl2 took place
to provide the desired TMS deprotected 6,7-epi-xylogiblacotone
A( 3, Table 2, entry 4). The structure of 3 was unambiguously
conﬁrmed by X-ray crystallography as shown in Figure 2.
The ﬁnal epoxidation of a chlorohydrin unit in 3 was
conducted under various basic conditions. However, reactions
always produced 1 along with a mixture of inseparable
diastereomers mainly due to an epimerization at C4 of the γ-
lactone unit.
17 Epoxidations at low temperatures turned out to
be ineﬃcient in terms of chemical conversion and purity in the
desired product. After intensive investigations for selective
epoxidation, it was gratifying to ﬁnd that the use of Ag
2O (1.0
equiv) in aqueous THF at 70 °C for 4 h proved to be optimal to
form the reported hypoxylactone ( 1) without producing the
epimer.18 Finally, NMR data of 1 was compared with the
reported data, but observed data did not match the reported
values.
3 The comparison results could suggest structural
incorrection of hypoxylactone ( 1) in the previous report.
In light of the above results that the stereoselective synthesis
of 1 turned out not to be a natural diastereomer of
hypoxylactone, we next drew attention to the application of
our approach for the synthesis of the natural hypoxylactone on
the basis of a hypothetical bio logical relationship with
xylogiblactone A ( 4). We undertook the synthesis of 9 starting
from aldehyde 8a (R = TBS), prepared from the previous
sequence for 7, as shown in Scheme 4. The allenoate γ-addition
reaction of 8a under similar conditions aﬀorded the γ-adduct 13
as a single regio- and stereoisomer in 75% yield. The reaction
underwent smoothly even at a lower temperature, −20 °C, after
an enolization of the allenoate 6 at −50 °C for 30 min. This
result shows a clear case of the matched reaction pair. That is,
reactivity and selectivity of the reaction can arise from the
matched case, anti-Felkin −Anh model D, favored in both
electronic and steric factors. With a possible connection
between (+)-xylogiblactone A ( 4) and hypoxylactone, γ-adduct
13 was carried out for a Au(I)-catalyzed (10 mol %) cyclization
to form the lactone 14 in 78% yield. Next, the TBS deprotection
of 14 was initially attempted with a basic ﬂuoride source, but the
γ-lactone moiety turned out to be sensitive to the basic ﬂuoride
causing epimerization at the C4 position of γ-lactone as

previously observed. After examining various conditions, the
TBS group was cleanly taken oﬀ with 10% aq HCl (5.5 equiv) in
MeOH at rt to result in (+)-xylogiblactone A ( 4).
Then, the resulting (+)-xylogiblactone A (4) was treated with
Ag2O (1.0 equiv) in aqueous THF at 70 °C to provide the
epoxide 9 as a sole product. Finally, we were delighted to ﬁnd
that all physical data of 9 including spectroscopic data were
identical with the original data.3 This outcome supports that the
stereochemical assignment of the epoxide in hypoxylactone
needs to be revised from 1 to 9. The result clearly shows
chemical and biological connections between hypoxylactone (9)
and xylogiblactone A ( 4).
In summary, we demonstrated not only facile syntheses of
(+)-xylogiblactone A ( 4) and hypoxylactone ( 9) by means of
the allenoate γ-additions but also structural revision of
hypoxylactone (1). According to the newly con ﬁrmed structure
of the natural γ-lactone 9, it also suggests that further veriﬁcation
of the structure of hypoxysordarin ( 2) will be necessary.
Stereochemistry of (+)-hypoxylactone is revised unambiguously
by the synthesis of both (+)-xylogiblactone A (4) and its epimer
3. Further studies are in progress for synthetic applications to
useful substances and evaluation of biological activities on
natural and unnatural γ-lactones.
■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
General. Unless otherwise stated, reactions were run in ﬂame-dried
glassware under an atmosphere of nitrogen or argon. Solvents were
dried by passage through an activated alumina column under argon.
Also, dichloromethane was distilled from P 2O5 prior to use. All liquid
reagents purchased from Aldrich or Alfa Aesar were distilled properly
prior to use, unless otherwise indicated. Triethylamine and
diisopropylethylamine were distilled from CaH 2 prior to use.
Puriﬁcation was conducted by ﬂash column chromatography on silica
gel (230 −400 mesh), eluting with a mixture of hexanes and ethyl
acetate, unless otherwise stated. The reported yields refer to
chromatographically puri ﬁed and isolated products. All reactions
were monitored by thin-layer chromatography carried out on Merck
silica gel plate (60 F
254) using UV light as a visualizing agent and
ethanolic anisaldehyde solution and heat as the developing agent. Silica
gel 60 (TA792685, 230 −400 mesh) from Merck was used for column
chromatography. The reported yields are for chromatographically pure
isolated products.
1H and 13C NMR spectra recorded on a Varian Unity
Inova (at 300 and 75 MHz, respectively), Bruker Advance-500 (at 500
and 125 MHz, respectively), and/or Agilent ProPulse 500 (at 500 and
125 MHz, respectively) are reported relative to residual proton solvent
(CDCl
3 = 7.26 and 77.0 ppm, respectively). Data for 1H NMR spectra
are reported as follows: chemical shift ( δ ppm) (multiplicity, coupling
constant in Hz, integration). NMR data were acquired at the Korea
Basic Science Institute (KBSI, Gwangju branch). IR spectra were
recorded on a Bruker Vertex 70 spectrometer and are reported in the

−1). High-resolution mass spectra
(HRMS) were acquired from the Korea Basic Science Institute

crystallography was performed by Dr. H. J. Lee at the Korea Basic
Science Institute (KBSI, Western Seoul branch).
All reported values are within 0.5% of the calculated value. Optical
rotations were measured on a PerkinElmer 343 plus at an ambient
temperature (Na line).
